topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; findings may have limited applicability to Australian healthcare settings, which have different regulatory frameworks, funding models, and organisational structures.
takeaways: Review identifies specific digital competencies needed in public health roles; use this to map which AI-related skills your health workforce currently lacks and prioritise targeted training.

European competency frameworks may require adaptation for Australian public health context — assess which components align with local healthcare governance, privacy regulations (e.g., Australian Privacy Act), and service delivery models before implementation.

Digital literacy frameworks in public health emphasise both technical skills and change management capabilities; ensure AI upskilling programmes address not just tools but also the cultural and organisational factors that support adoption.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education competencies. While the framework-development methodology may transfer to other health professions, the dental-specific technical and clinical competencies will not generalise to non-healthcare fields or broader AI literacy contexts.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for AI should distinguish between foundational literacy (what all learners need), domain-specific technical skills (e.g., interpreting AI outputs in diagnostics), and ethical/regulatory competencies — this tiered approach can guide your own capability-building priorities.

Embedding AI competencies early in professional education (rather than as an add-on) increases integration with core discipline knowledge — consider how to weave AI literacy into existing workflows and role requirements rather than treating it as separate training.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on middle school education curriculum design. Applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development depends on how well secondary education frameworks translate to organisational contexts.
takeaways: Consider scaffolding AI competencies within a broader digital literacy framework rather than teaching AI skills in isolation — this holistic approach may improve retention and contextual understanding for adult learners too.

Identify which AI competencies are foundational (e.g., understanding algorithmic bias, data literacy) versus advanced, to design tiered upskilling programmes that meet diverse employee starting points.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development; generalisability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without full article review.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI integration often stems from knowledge gaps rather than principled opposition; targeted upskilling programs can shift mindset from resistance to readiness.
Structured faculty development should precede or accompany AI literacy initiatives for students — educators must understand AI tools and their limitations before teaching others.

Public health curricula may require sector-specific AI literacy frameworks that address domain-relevant applications (epidemiology, policy analysis, data governance) rather than generic AI competencies.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to be a conceptual/theoretical review of educational strategies for AI literacy in Gen Z. Generalisability depends on whether examples draw from specific regions or sectors; without access to the full article, geographic scope and applicability to Australian educational contexts cannot be fully assessed.
takeaways: Identify which innovative educational strategies (e.g. project-based learning, cross-disciplinary modules, industry partnerships) are most effective for building AI literacy in younger cohorts, then pilot them in your organisation's graduate or early-career development programmes.

Map the specific AI skills gaps in your workforce by role and generation, then design targeted upskilling pathways that account for Gen Z's learning preferences and career expectations around AI-adjacent roles.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific methodologies, sample composition, and regional applicability are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation—prioritise reskilling and role redesign alongside tool deployment.
Develop targeted AI literacy programmes that address different job functions and career stages, recognising that transformation success depends on employee readiness, not technology readiness alone.
Build change management infrastructure early: identify which roles will shift, which will emerge, and which will become obsolete—then design transition support accordingly.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — the snippet provides insufficient detail on study design, sample characteristics, geography, or methodology to assess generalisability. The theoretical framework (psychological capital in AI-driven workplaces) may have broad relevance, but actual applicability depends on unstated sample composition and context.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (self-efficacy, hope, resilience, optimism) in your team as a precursor to leveraging AI as a job resource rather than a threat — this may unlock innovation outcomes in algorithm-driven roles.

When introducing AI tools, frame them explicitly as job resources that expand capability rather than replace workers; doing so may activate the psychological conditions needed for employees to experiment and innovate.

Assess and invest in team members' belief in their ability to work effectively with AI systems — self-efficacy appears to be a critical mechanism linking psychological capital to innovation in AI-augmented work.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing populations and healthcare settings with medical AI implementation. Generalisability to other sectors or professions may be limited, though the autonomy-wellbeing mechanism could be relevant across knowledge work domains.
takeaways: Protect and clarify work autonomy during AI implementation: nurses' wellbeing depends not just on AI readiness training, but on maintaining control over how AI tools are used in their daily practice—design implementation to preserve decision-making authority.

Use autonomy as a leading indicator: monitor perceived autonomy alongside AI readiness metrics during rollout; declining autonomy signals emerging wellbeing risks, even if technical competence is strong.

Frame AI readiness through an autonomy lens: structure training and change communication to emphasise how AI augments rather than replaces professional judgment, helping staff see themselves as agents, not merely tool users.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — raises conceptual concerns about employee AI use patterns, but lacks empirical data on prevalence, sectors, or geographies affected. Likely reflects perspectives most relevant to large knowledge-worker organisations in developed economies.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational guidelines on appropriate use of AI tools for personal versus work matters to reduce psychological dependency and data privacy risks.

Create awareness programs highlighting potential downsides of over-reliance on AI for emotional or professional support (e.g., isolation, reduced peer connection, algorithmic bias in advice), and direct employees to human resources or EAP alternatives.
Audit which AI tools employees are using for work and personal purposes, and ensure managers can recognise signs of unhealthy AI dependency that might affect workplace wellbeing and performance.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) is likely applicable across sectors, but geographic scope and organisational contexts are unclear.
takeaways: The Automation–Augmentation Paradox suggests generative AI adoption creates competing risks: employees may become passive knowledge consumers (automation effect) or develop deeper expertise through augmented capabilities—intentional workplace design is needed to encourage the latter outcome.
Consider structuring AI implementation to preserve critical thinking and knowledge-building activities rather than replacing them, as passive AI reliance may erode employee expertise over time.

Monitor whether AI adoption in your organisation is driving employees toward learning and capability development or toward dependency on automated outputs—this distinction is critical for long-term workforce capability.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, and sector not indicated. Findings on paternalistic leadership effects may be culturally influenced and require context on whether study was conducted in cultures where this leadership style is prevalent.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership among employees by involving them in AI implementation decisions — those who feel they 'own' AI tools are more likely to actively collaborate with them rather than resist or disengage.
Create structured opportunities for 'AI crafting' (customising AI tools to individual or team needs) as a mechanism to strengthen both psychological ownership and actual collaboration behaviours.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, emphasise the leader's supportive intent when introducing AI, as employees' sense of protection and care from leadership may amplify their willingness to adopt AI-based workflows.

articles.title: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on conceptual analysis rather than empirical research. Findings likely apply broadly to knowledge workers in developed economies, but specific contextual factors (industry, organisational culture, AI tool maturity) may affect applicability.
takeaways: Identify which employee segments in your organisation are most likely to benefit from AI for creative work — this varies based on individual factors like cognitive style, experience level, and comfort with technology, so a one-size-fits-all implementation will underperform.

Design targeted onboarding and support mechanisms: employees who struggle with AI-enhanced creativity may need different training, clearer use cases, or different tools than those who naturally thrive with AI augmentation.

Monitor whether AI is widening or narrowing creative capability gaps within teams — use this insight to adjust allocation of AI tools and training to ensure equitable access to creativity-boosting benefits.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights based on consulting experience, likely skewed toward large organisations and developed economies. Specific applicability to Australian SMEs or public sector contexts not established.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (one-time event) to 'AI adaptation' (ongoing behavioural change) to sustain engagement and capability building beyond initial rollout.

Design change interventions that explicitly target the human behaviours needed for AI use (e.g., learning to prompt, data literacy, comfort with algorithmic decision-making) rather than assuming technical training alone drives adoption.
Tailor change approaches to different workforce segments and roles, since AI adaptation demands vary by job function and existing digital maturity.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — Stanford GSB perspective reflects primarily US business context and may not account for different labour markets, regulations, or workplace cultures in Australia and other regions.
takeaways: Identify specific workplace tasks and roles most vulnerable to AI disruption in your organisation, then develop targeted upskilling programs before changes occur rather than reacting afterwards.

Create transparent communication channels about AI implementation timelines and job implications — employees who understand how AI will change their work are more likely to engage constructively with change initiatives.

Map which existing skills will remain valuable (e.g., complex problem-solving, interpersonal communication) and build behaviour-change strategies that position AI as a tool that augments rather than replaces human capability.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings could be limited by specific organisational contexts or geographic regions not indicated.
takeaways: Employees' job crafting responses to AI adoption vary based on whether they perceive AI as an opportunity (approach) or a threat (avoidance) — understanding these individual differences helps tailor change management strategies to support positive adaptation.

Organisational leaders can proactively shape job crafting outcomes by framing AI adoption in ways that emphasise skill development and new role possibilities rather than job loss, thereby shifting employees toward approach-oriented behaviours.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodological details are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption requires deliberate workforce transformation strategy, not just technology implementation; plan changes to roles, skills, and organizational structure in parallel with AI rollout.
Frame AI capability development as a behaviour change initiative affecting how employees work, not merely an IT deployment—this shifts focus to mindset, training readiness, and change management.
Identify which workforce segments will experience the most significant role shifts and design targeted support (reskilling, redeployment pathways) to sustain engagement during transition.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to Chinese primary and secondary school teachers and may not generalise to other cultural contexts, educational systems, or sectors. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference.
takeaways: AI adoption in education produces paradoxical effects: perceived as both opportunity and threat to teacher autonomy. Organisations should actively frame AI as complementary to teaching rather than replacement to mitigate threat responses that undermine innovation adoption.

Teachers' psychological appraisal of AI (challenge vs. threat mindset) is a critical lever for behaviour change — those viewing AI as a challenge show higher innovative teaching behaviour. Use framing, training, and messaging that emphasises skill-building and teacher agency to shift this perception.

Simply providing AI tools is insufficient; change management must address underlying beliefs about competence and control. Invest in support systems and leadership communication that validate teacher expertise while positioning AI as extending rather than diminishing their role.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but specific organisational contexts and implementation details may vary. Findings are most directly applicable to large enterprises with resources for structured change programmes.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a standalone training initiative but as a core organisational change programme with clear business outcomes, sponsorship, and integration into existing change management processes.
Design AI capability development around change readiness: assess employee mindsets, resistance patterns, and readiness for role transformation before launching technical training.
Embed AI upskilling into performance management, career pathways, and incentive systems so it becomes a change expectation rather than optional professional development.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New study reveals an unexpected difference between casual and compulsive pornography viewers - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New study reveals an unexpected difference between casual and compulsive pornography viewers  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unknown — snippet provides insufficient detail about study design, sample size, geography, or methodology to assess generalisability.
takeaways: The headline suggests a counterintuitive finding that distinguishes casual from compulsive viewers, but the mechanism or nature of the difference remains mysterious from this snippet alone.

This touches on behavioural differences that might reveal something surprising about habit formation, impulse control, or neurological responses — exactly the kind of finding that challenges everyday assumptions.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone — unclear whether findings apply across cultures, age groups, or contexts.
takeaways: People with different personality traits don't all remember surprising moments the same way — some personalities appear 'wired' to lock in unexpected events better than others.
Your personality might explain why you vividly recall that awkward meeting moment while your colleague forgot it instantly — it's not just about how shocking the event was, but who you are.
The interplay between personality and surprise suggests memory isn't a passive recording device; it's shaped by the psychological traits we bring to an experience.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — typical neuroscience news reporting often covers single studies with small samples; scope and population details unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Brain imaging research has identified measurable neurological differences in people with psychopathic traits, suggesting the condition has biological foundations rather than being purely behavioural.

The 'shocking difference' angle highlights how neuroscience can make abstract psychological traits visible and concrete — making the unfamiliar brain architecture behind personality differences genuinely surprising to most people.
Findings like this remind us that conditions we think of as purely psychological often have fascinating hardware-level explanations, which can shift how we think about responsibility and treatment.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear — this is a news report summarising research findings without sufficient detail about the original study's sample, methodology, or geographic scope to assess generalisability.
takeaways: People high in antagonistic narcissism (dominance, entitlement, callousness) apparently attract romantic partners despite — or perhaps because of — traits we'd normally expect to repel people.

The finding flips common intuitions: behaviours that seem actively off-putting (aggression, lack of empathy, self-centredness) can paradoxically create romantic appeal, suggesting attraction works through different psychological mechanisms than we assume.

This research reminds us that human mate selection involves complex, sometimes counterintuitive drives that don't always align with what makes for healthy relationships — a fascinating window into how evolution and psychology shape attraction.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — claims of global patterns suggest large cross-cultural sample, though specific sample size and methodology are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: People's taste in music is a surprisingly reliable window into their personality — suggesting that whether someone loves jazz, metal, or pop might reveal more about who they are than they realise.
Personality-music links appear consistent across cultures, hinting that some aspects of human psychology and aesthetic preference are genuinely universal rather than culturally constructed.

This finding is counterintuitive because music is often thought of as deeply cultural, yet personality seems to transcend those boundaries — your favourite song might say more about your openness to experience than your country of origin.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — depends on the wine review dataset used and whether findings generalise across different wine cultures, regions, and reviewer demographics. Results may be specific to English-language reviews or particular platforms.
takeaways: People's wine descriptions reveal personality traits — an AI detected links between how someone describes wine (vocabulary, adjectives, tone) and their underlying personality, suggesting our everyday writing contains subtle psychological fingerprints.

Language patterns in casual reviews can be surprisingly predictive — this hints at how AI might infer personality from any written content (reviews, emails, social media), raising interesting questions about what we inadvertently reveal online.

Wine reviewing is a window into human perception — the fact that wine descriptions correlate with personality suggests that taste preferences and how we articulate them aren't just about the wine itself, but shaped by who we are.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on academic settings and multicultural teams; findings may not generalise to non-academic sectors or homogeneous workgroups. Sample and methodological details unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to nudge leaders toward more inclusive behaviours, potentially reducing gender bias in team dynamics — consider piloting AI-assisted feedback systems in your leadership development programmes.

Inclusive leadership practices in multicultural teams require intentional design; AI-assisted prompts may help leaders recognise and address blind spots around gender equity that arise in diverse group settings.

Monitor whether AI recommendations actually shift team outcomes (psychological safety, contribution equity) rather than just leadership awareness — measure whether team members, especially women and minorities, report feeling safer and more valued.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but with typical survey limitations — findings reflect PwC's respondent base (likely skewed toward white-collar, professionally engaged workers) and snapshot perceptions rather than longitudinal trends. Generalisability varies by country and sector within the global sample.
takeaways: Identify specific workplace fears (job security, AI displacement, workload, management trust) from the 2025 data to tailor psychological safety interventions — fears left unaddressed erode trust and inhibit speaking up.

Use hopes and fears data segmented by country/role to design targeted communication and support; misalignment between what employees hope for and what organisations deliver is a psychological safety red flag.

Monitor shifts in hope/fear ratios as leading indicators of psychological safety; declining hope or rising fears warrant proactive culture and leadership interventions before engagement and retention suffer.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical model (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may apply broadly, but geographic scope, sector diversity, and sample size are unclear from available information.
takeaways: AI adoption can undermine psychological safety if not paired with explicit ethical leadership — leaders must actively communicate values and create space for employees to voice concerns about AI implementation without fear of consequences.

Monitor employee mental health during AI transitions; depression and reduced psychological safety may be early warning signs that implementation is creating anxiety or exclusion rather than capability-building.

Ethical leadership practices (transparency, fairness, accountability in AI decisions) appear to be a critical moderator — invest in leader training on how to implement AI in ways that maintain or strengthen psychological safety rather than eroding it.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on global consulting experience and client work, but specific sample details, methodology, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect practices in larger organisations across developed economies.
takeaways: Create explicit norms and practices that actively reduce status differences and power dynamics, enabling quieter or junior employees to contribute ideas without fear of embarrassment or retribution.

Use structured feedback mechanisms and inclusive meeting practices (e.g., round-robin input, anonymous suggestion channels) to surface ideas from employees who might otherwise self-silence due to perceived organisational hierarchy.

Measure psychological safety regularly through pulse surveys and focus groups to identify which teams or functions lack safety, then target interventions to those groups rather than applying one-size-fits-all approaches.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — guidance reflects US HR practice norms and SHRM's US-focused membership, but core psychological safety principles are broadly applicable across geographies and sectors.
takeaways: Identify the specific four leadership practices SHRM recommends (from the article) and implement them systematically in your team meetings and one-on-ones to establish baseline psychological safety behaviours.
Use this as a diagnostic tool: assess your current team against each of the four ways to pinpoint which psychological safety dimensions need attention, then prioritise the biggest gap first.
Share the framework with your leadership peer group to create consistent language and expectations around psychological safety across your organisation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — sample size, geography, and sector not specified. Generalisability depends on whether study includes diverse industries and workforce demographics.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key lever for helping employees innovate when working alongside AI — consider assessing and building these capacities in your team as you introduce AI tools.

Frame AI as a 'job resource' rather than a threat or replacement in your communication and change management — this mindset shift may unlock greater psychological capital and willingness to experiment with new capabilities.
